entries.condition: Recent 'Bug Patch' or similar commit in git history, Test files removed in separate 'Remove F2P Tests' commit, Simple revert or restoration would fix the issue, Bug is visible in git diff of recent commits
entries.strategy: For issues with recent 'Bug Patch' commits: Check git history early (within first 5 steps) to identify intentional bug injections. Use `git checkout <commit>~1 -- <file>` to restore specific files rather than `git revert`, which creates merge state. Fix ONLY production code files - do NOT restore test files unless explicitly required for verification.

entries.condition: Test files were restored during debugging/verification, Agent used `git checkout` to restore files, Multiple files modified including tests, Evaluation harness applies its own test patches
entries.strategy: Before submission, verify `git status` shows ONLY intended production code changes. If test files were restored for verification, explicitly unstage them with `git restore --staged <file>` or remove them from the working tree. Never submit with staged test files or new test files in the working directory.

entries.condition: Simple logic bugs or obvious errors, Bug location identified early, Agent shows signs of over-exploration or repeated analysis, No complex multi-file dependencies
entries.strategy: Use explicit phase boundaries (LOCATE → UNDERSTAND → FIX) with step budgets to prevent analysis paralysis. After locating the bug (typically 5-10 steps), transition to fixing rather than continuing exploration. For simple bugs, avoid re-verification loops that delay action.

entries.condition: Functionality completely missing (not just buggy), Recent commits show code deletions, Error suggests recent regression, Working implementation may exist in git history
entries.strategy: For bugs where git history reveals deleted or modified code: Prompt agents to check `git log` and `git show` in the LOCATE phase, especially when functionality is completely missing rather than buggy. Compare current code with recent commits when features appear entirely absent.

entries.condition: Tests pass cleanly after fix, Fix is a simple revert or restoration, Agent has already run relevant tests, No complex multi-component changes
entries.strategy: When tests pass after applying a fix (especially git reverts), encourage immediate submission rather than additional verification loops. Avoid 'CRITICAL' or 'ALWAYS verify' language that creates hesitation when the agent has already confirmed success with passing tests.

entries.condition: Code pattern appears multiple times in codebase, Risk of unintended changes to similar code, Surgical precision required, Pattern-based editing needed
entries.strategy: For issues with repeated code patterns: Use line-specific editing (sed with line numbers, or nl+sed) rather than broad text replacement. ALWAYS verify edits with `git diff` immediately after making changes to ensure only intended locations were modified.

entries.condition: Bug spans multiple files, Requires understanding test framework conventions, Similar working code exists elsewhere, Exploration across different code areas needed
entries.strategy: For multi-file bugs requiring exploration across source, tests, and git history: Provide command examples showing BOTH exploration patterns (e.g., 'grep -r X . | head -20 OR git log -p') in initial guidance. Use comparative analysis early - when one implementation is broken, immediately compare with working similar code in the same codebase.

entries.condition: Single commit introduced multiple related bugs, Changes span multiple methods or classes, All bugs trace to one commit, Clean revert is possible
entries.strategy: When git history reveals a bug-introducing commit that modified multiple related components, prefer atomic file-level reverts (`git checkout <commit> -- <file>`) over manual line-by-line edits. This ensures all related changes are reverted together, preventing partial fixes.

entries.condition: Bug requires changes in multiple locations, Pattern-based bug (e.g., float vs Decimal usage), Coordinated changes needed across files, Risk of partial fixes
entries.strategy: For precision/arithmetic bugs requiring coordinated multi-file changes: After locating the bug pattern, immediately identify ALL occurrences across the codebase before fixing. Apply fixes in a single focused burst rather than incremental exploration. Batch import changes with method updates together.

entries.condition: Multiple test failures present, Some failures may be environmental, Need to distinguish bug-related from pre-existing failures, Container or CI environment issues possible
entries.strategy: When pytest shows failures, check if they're related to the actual bug or environmental/pre-existing issues. Run pytest WITHOUT fail-fast flags (-x) first to see the full test landscape. Test the specific reproduction case from the issue description directly before debugging unrelated failures.

entries.condition: Test files were deleted, Existing tests may provide coverage, Full test suite is slow or may timeout, Verification needed but test restoration risky
entries.strategy: Use broad test discovery (`pytest tests/ -k <keyword>`) BEFORE attempting to restore specific deleted test files. Only restore deleted tests if broad discovery finds insufficient coverage. Prefer lightweight verification (simple reproduction scripts) over full test suite runs that may timeout.

entries.condition: Issue description may be outdated, Code may have been fixed already, Reproduction steps don't show expected behavior, All tests pass from the beginning
entries.strategy: Verify the issue actually exists before attempting to fix it. When reproduction steps don't produce the expected error, explicitly state 'issue cannot be reproduced' or 'issue appears already fixed' rather than proceeding with analysis.

general_notes: Soft nudges outperform hard gates (reflection prompts +2pp, submission gates -8pp).
Do not modify has_finished() — over-specification drops pass rate.
Strategies are grounded in contrastive trajectory analysis: same issue, different harness, different agent behavior.
anti_patterns: Restoring test files during the fix phase and submitting them with production code changes - evaluation harnesses apply their own test patches and will reject submissions with test file modifications
Using `git revert` instead of `git checkout <commit>~1 -- <file>` for reverting bug patches - revert creates merge state and may stage unintended files
Continuing extensive exploration after the bug is located and understood - this leads to analysis paralysis and timeout without adding value
Using broad text replacement (sed without line numbers) on patterns that appear multiple times in the codebase - this causes unintended changes to similar code
Running pytest with fail-fast flags (-x, -xvs) when multiple test failures exist - this stops at the first failure which may be environmental/unrelated, hiding the actual bug-related test results
Over-verification after tests pass - adding 'CRITICAL' verification requirements when the agent has already confirmed the fix works creates unnecessary hesitation and delays submission
Providing explicit 'echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT' commands in prompts - agents may execute this prematurely before actually completing the work
